E-News Express Project¶

Business Statistics — A/B Testing & Hypothesis Testing¶

Course: Applied Statistics — Great Learning PG Program in AI & ML Total Marks: 60

1. Defining the Problem & Exploratory Data Analysis¶

1.1 Business Context¶

The advent of e-news, or electronic news, portals has offered us a great opportunity to quickly get updates on the day-to-day events occurring globally. The information on these portals is retrieved electronically from online databases, processed using a variety of software, and then transmitted to the users. There are multiple advantages of transmitting news electronically, like faster access to the content and the ability to utilize different technologies such as audio, graphics, video, and other interactive elements that are either not being used or aren't common yet in traditional newspapers.

E-News Express, an online news portal, aims to expand its business by acquiring new subscribers. With every visitor to the website taking certain actions based on their interest, the company plans to analyze these actions to understand user interests and determine how to drive better engagement. The executives at E-News Express believe that there has been a decline in new monthly subscribers compared to the past year because the current webpage is not designed well enough in terms of the outline & recommended content to keep customers engaged long enough to decide to subscribe.

Companies often analyze user responses to two variants of a product to decide which of the two variants is more effective. This experimental technique, known as A/B testing, is used to determine whether a new feature attracts users based on a chosen metric.

1.2 Objective¶

The design team of the company has researched and created a new landing page that has a new outline & more relevant content compared to the old page. To test the effectiveness of the new landing page in gathering new subscribers, the Data Science team experimented by randomly selecting 100 users and dividing them equally into two groups:

  • The existing landing page was served to the first group (control group)
  • The new landing page was served to the second group (treatment group)

Data regarding the interaction of users in both groups with the two versions of the landing page was collected.

1.3 Questions to be Answered¶

At a significance level of 5% (α = 0.05), we need to determine the effectiveness of the new landing page by answering:

  1. Do the users spend more time on the new landing page than on the existing landing page?
  2. Is the conversion rate (the proportion of users who visit the landing page and get converted) for the new page greater than the conversion rate for the old page?
  3. Does the converted status depend on the preferred language?
  4. Is the time spent on the new page the same for the different language users?

1.4 Data Dictionary¶

Column Description
user_id Unique user ID of the person visiting the website
group Whether the user belongs to the first group (control) or the second group (treatment)
landing_page Whether the landing page is new or old
time_spent_on_the_page Time (in minutes) spent by the user on the landing page
converted Whether the user gets converted to a subscriber of the news portal or not
language_preferred Language chosen by the user to view the landing page

2. Key Insights from Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Observations on Individual Variables:¶

  1. Balanced Experimental Design: The A/B test has a perfect 50-50 split between control and treatment groups, ensuring a fair comparison.

  2. Overall Conversion Rate: 54% of users across both groups converted to subscribers, indicating reasonable overall engagement.

  3. Language Distribution: Spanish (34) and French (34) are equally the most preferred languages, followed by English (32). The fairly even distribution allows for meaningful cross-language analysis.

  4. Time Spent Distribution: The overall time spent on the page ranges from 0.19 to 10.71 minutes, with a slight right skew — most users spend between 2-8 minutes on the page.

Observations on Relationships Between Variables:¶

  1. Time Spent vs Group: Users on the new landing page spend considerably more time (mean ≈ 6.22 min) compared to the old page (mean ≈ 4.53 min). The treatment group also shows lower variability, suggesting more consistent engagement.

  2. Conversion vs Group: The new page shows a 24-percentage-point higher conversion rate (66% vs 42%). This is a substantial practical difference.

  3. Conversion vs Language: Conversion rates appear relatively similar across all three languages, suggesting that the landing page effectiveness may be language-agnostic.

  4. Time vs Language (New Page): Among users who saw the new page, mean time spent appears similar across languages, though formal testing is needed.

These visual observations suggest the new landing page is more effective, but we need to confirm this through formal statistical hypothesis testing at α = 0.05.

3. Hypothesis Test 1: Do users spend more time on the new landing page?¶

Question: Do the users spend more time on the new landing page than on the existing landing page?

3.1 Visual Analysis¶

3.2 Hypotheses Formulation¶

  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ_new ≤ μ_old — The mean time spent on the new landing page is less than or equal to the mean time spent on the old landing page.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): μ_new > μ_old — The mean time spent on the new landing page is greater than the mean time spent on the old landing page.

3.3 Selecting the Appropriate Test¶

Since we are comparing the means of two independent groups (control vs treatment), we will use the Independent Samples t-test (one-tailed, right-tailed). Before applying the t-test, we will verify the assumptions of normality and homogeneity of variances.

In [19]:
# --- Data Collection and Preparation ---
control_time = df[df['group'] == 'control']['time_spent_on_the_page']
treatment_time = df[df['group'] == 'treatment']['time_spent_on_the_page']

print("Sample Statistics:")
print(f"  Control (Old Page):   n = {len(control_time)}, Mean = {control_time.mean():.4f}, Std = {control_time.std():.4f}")
print(f"  Treatment (New Page): n = {len(treatment_time)}, Mean = {treatment_time.mean():.4f}, Std = {treatment_time.std():.4f}")

# --- Assumption Check 1: Normality (Shapiro-Wilk Test) ---
print("\n--- Normality Check (Shapiro-Wilk Test) ---")
print("H₀: The data follows a normal distribution")
print("H₁: The data does not follow a normal distribution")

stat_c, p_c = shapiro(control_time)
stat_t, p_t = shapiro(treatment_time)
print(f"\n  Control group:   W = {stat_c:.4f}, p-value = {p_c:.4f}", end="")
print(f"  → {'Fail to reject H₀ (Normal)' if p_c > 0.05 else 'Reject H₀ (Not Normal)'}")
print(f"  Treatment group: W = {stat_t:.4f}, p-value = {p_t:.4f}", end="")
print(f"  → {'Fail to reject H₀ (Normal)' if p_t > 0.05 else 'Reject H₀ (Not Normal)'}")

# --- Assumption Check 2: Homogeneity of Variances (Levene's Test) ---
print("\n--- Homogeneity of Variances (Levene's Test) ---")
print("H₀: The variances of the two groups are equal")
print("H₁: The variances of the two groups are not equal")

stat_l, p_l = levene(control_time, treatment_time)
print(f"\n  Levene's statistic = {stat_l:.4f}, p-value = {p_l:.4f}", end="")
print(f"  → {'Equal variances (use pooled t-test)' if p_l > 0.05 else 'Unequal variances (use Welch t-test)'}")

equal_var = p_l > 0.05

Sample Statistics:
  Control (Old Page):   n = 50, Mean = 4.5324, Std = 2.5820
  Treatment (New Page): n = 50, Mean = 6.2232, Std = 1.8170

--- Normality Check (Shapiro-Wilk Test) ---
H₀: The data follows a normal distribution
H₁: The data does not follow a normal distribution

  Control group:   W = 0.9776, p-value = 0.4561  → Fail to reject H₀ (Normal)
  Treatment group: W = 0.9858, p-value = 0.8040  → Fail to reject H₀ (Normal)

--- Homogeneity of Variances (Levene's Test) ---
H₀: The variances of the two groups are equal
H₁: The variances of the two groups are not equal

  Levene's statistic = 7.1137, p-value = 0.0090  → Unequal variances (use Welch t-test)
In [20]:
# --- Performing the t-test ---
# Using appropriate t-test based on Levene's test result
test_type = "Pooled t-test" if equal_var else "Welch's t-test"
print(f"Selected Test: Independent Samples {test_type} (One-tailed, Right-tailed)")
print(f"Significance Level: α = 0.05\n")

t_stat, p_value_two_tailed = ttest_ind(treatment_time, control_time, equal_var=equal_var)
# For one-tailed test (right-tailed: treatment > control), divide by 2
p_value = p_value_two_tailed / 2

print(f"--- Test Results ---")
print(f"  t-statistic:           {t_stat:.4f}")
print(f"  p-value (two-tailed):  {p_value_two_tailed:.6f}")
print(f"  p-value (one-tailed):  {p_value:.6f}")

# --- Inference ---
print(f"\n--- Inference ---")
if t_stat > 0 and p_value < 0.05:
    print(f"  Since the p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is LESS than α (0.05) and t-statistic is positive,")
    print(f"  we REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✓ Conclusion: At 5% significance level, there is sufficient statistical evidence")
    print(f"    to conclude that users spend MORE time on the new landing page than on the old")
    print(f"    landing page. The new page increases user engagement time.")
else:
    print(f"  Since the p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is GREATER than or equal to α (0.05),")
    print(f"  we FAIL TO REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✗ Conclusion: There is insufficient evidence to conclude that users spend more")
    print(f"    time on the new landing page.")

Selected Test: Independent Samples Welch's t-test (One-tailed, Right-tailed)
Significance Level: α = 0.05

--- Test Results ---
  t-statistic:           3.7868
  p-value (two-tailed):  0.000278
  p-value (one-tailed):  0.000139

--- Inference ---
  Since the p-value (0.000139) is LESS than α (0.05) and t-statistic is positive,
  we REJECT the Null Hypothesis.

  ✓ Conclusion: At 5% significance level, there is sufficient statistical evidence
    to conclude that users spend MORE time on the new landing page than on the old
    landing page. The new page increases user engagement time.

4. Hypothesis Test 2: Is the conversion rate for the new page greater?¶

Question: Is the conversion rate (the proportion of users who visit the landing page and get converted) for the new page greater than the conversion rate for the old page?

4.1 Visual Analysis¶

In [21]:
# Visual comparison of conversion rates
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Grouped count plot
conv_ct = pd.crosstab(df['group'], df['converted'])
conv_ct.plot(kind='bar', ax=axes[0], color=['#e78ac3', '#8da0cb'],
             edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.8, width=0.6)
axes[0].set_title('Conversion Counts by Group', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Group')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Number of Users')
axes[0].legend(title='Converted')
axes[0].set_xticklabels(axes[0].get_xticklabels(), rotation=0)

# Proportions comparison with reference line
conv_rates = df.groupby('group')['converted'].apply(lambda x: (x == 'yes').mean()) * 100
axes[1].bar(conv_rates.index, conv_rates.values, color=['#66c2a5', '#fc8d62'],
            edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.8, width=0.5)
axes[1].axhline(y=50, color='gray', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5, label='50% line')
axes[1].set_title('Conversion Rate: Old vs New Page', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Group')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Conversion Rate (%)')
for i, v in enumerate(conv_rates.values):
    axes[1].text(i, v + 1.5, f'{v:.0f}%', ha='center', fontweight='bold', fontsize=14)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 80)
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# The visual clearly shows the treatment group (new page) has a substantially higher
# conversion rate compared to the control group (old page).

4.2 Hypotheses Formulation¶

  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): p_new ≤ p_old — The conversion rate of the new page is less than or equal to the conversion rate of the old page.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): p_new > p_old — The conversion rate of the new page is greater than the conversion rate of the old page.

4.3 Selecting the Appropriate Test¶

Since we are comparing proportions from two independent groups, we will use the Two-Proportion Z-test (one-tailed, right-tailed).

In [22]:
# --- Data Collection and Preparation ---
n_control = len(df[df['group'] == 'control'])
n_treatment = len(df[df['group'] == 'treatment'])

converted_control = (df[df['group'] == 'control']['converted'] == 'yes').sum()
converted_treatment = (df[df['group'] == 'treatment']['converted'] == 'yes').sum()

p_control = converted_control / n_control
p_treatment = converted_treatment / n_treatment

print("Sample Proportions:")
print(f"  Control (Old Page):   {converted_control}/{n_control} = {p_control:.4f} ({p_control*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"  Treatment (New Page): {converted_treatment}/{n_treatment} = {p_treatment:.4f} ({p_treatment*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"  Difference:           {(p_treatment - p_control)*100:.1f} percentage points")

# --- Performing the Two-Proportion Z-test ---
print(f"\nSelected Test: Two-Proportion Z-test (One-tailed, Right-tailed)")
print(f"Significance Level: α = 0.05\n")

# Using statsmodels proportions_ztest
count = np.array([converted_treatment, converted_control])
nobs = np.array([n_treatment, n_control])

z_stat, p_value = proportions_ztest(count, nobs, alternative='larger')

print(f"--- Test Results ---")
print(f"  z-statistic:          {z_stat:.4f}")
print(f"  p-value (one-tailed): {p_value:.6f}")

# --- Inference ---
print(f"\n--- Inference ---")
if p_value < 0.05:
    print(f"  Since the p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is LESS than α (0.05),")
    print(f"  we REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✓ Conclusion: At 5% significance level, there is sufficient statistical evidence")
    print(f"    to conclude that the conversion rate of the new landing page is GREATER than")
    print(f"    the conversion rate of the old landing page.")
else:
    print(f"  Since the p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is GREATER than or equal to α (0.05),")
    print(f"  we FAIL TO REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✗ Conclusion: There is insufficient evidence to conclude that the new page")
    print(f"    has a higher conversion rate.")

5. Hypothesis Test 3: Does the converted status depend on the preferred language?¶

Question: Does the converted status depend on the preferred language?

5.1 Visual Analysis¶

Contingency Table:
converted           no  yes
language_preferred         
English             11   21
French              19   15
Spanish             16   18

5.2 Hypotheses Formulation¶

  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): The converted status is independent of the preferred language. (There is no association between language preference and conversion status.)
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): The converted status is dependent on the preferred language. (There is an association between language preference and conversion status.)

5.3 Selecting the Appropriate Test¶

Since we are testing the independence between two categorical variables (converted status and language preference), we will use the Chi-Square Test of Independence.

In [24]:
# --- Data Collection and Preparation ---
# Creating the contingency table
contingency_table = pd.crosstab(df['language_preferred'], df['converted'])
print("Observed Frequencies (Contingency Table):")
print(contingency_table)

# --- Performing the Chi-Square Test ---
print(f"\nSelected Test: Chi-Square Test of Independence")
print(f"Significance Level: α = 0.05\n")

chi2_stat, p_value, dof, expected_freq = chi2_contingency(contingency_table)

# Displaying expected frequencies
print("Expected Frequencies (under H₀ of independence):")
expected_df = pd.DataFrame(expected_freq,
                           index=contingency_table.index,
                           columns=contingency_table.columns)
print(expected_df.round(2))

# Checking assumption: all expected frequencies should be >= 5
min_expected = expected_freq.min()
print(f"\nMinimum expected frequency: {min_expected:.2f}")
if min_expected >= 5:
    print("All expected frequencies are ≥ 5 — Chi-Square test is valid.")
else:
    print("WARNING: Some expected frequencies < 5 — consider Fisher's exact test.")

print(f"\n--- Test Results ---")
print(f"  Chi-Square statistic: {chi2_stat:.4f}")
print(f"  Degrees of freedom:   {dof}")
print(f"  p-value:              {p_value:.6f}")

# --- Inference ---
print(f"\n--- Inference ---")
if p_value < 0.05:
    print(f"  Since the p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is LESS than α (0.05),")
    print(f"  we REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✓ Conclusion: At 5% significance level, there is sufficient evidence")
    print(f"    that the converted status DEPENDS on the preferred language.")
else:
    print(f"  Since the p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is GREATER than or equal to α (0.05),")
    print(f"  we FAIL TO REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✗ Conclusion: At 5% significance level, there is insufficient evidence")
    print(f"    to conclude that conversion status depends on language preference.")
    print(f"    The converted status appears to be INDEPENDENT of language preference.")

6. Hypothesis Test 4: Is the mean time spent on the new page the same for different language users?¶

Question: Is the time spent on the new page the same for the different language users?

6.1 Visual Analysis¶

In [25]:

axes[2].legend()

plt.show()

# The visual analysis suggests that the mean time spent on the new page
# is relatively similar across language groups.

6.2 Hypotheses Formulation¶

  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ_English = μ_Spanish = μ_French — The mean time spent on the new page is the same for all language groups.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): At least one language group has a different mean time spent on the new page.

6.3 Selecting the Appropriate Test¶

Since we are comparing means across more than two independent groups, we will use the One-Way ANOVA test. Before applying ANOVA, we will verify the assumptions of normality and homogeneity of variances.

In [26]:
# --- Data Collection and Preparation ---
treatment_df = df[df['group'] == 'treatment']

eng_time = treatment_df[treatment_df['language_preferred'] == 'English']['time_spent_on_the_page']
spa_time = treatment_df[treatment_df['language_preferred'] == 'Spanish']['time_spent_on_the_page']
fre_time = treatment_df[treatment_df['language_preferred'] == 'French']['time_spent_on_the_page']

print("Sample Statistics (Treatment Group — New Page Only):")
print(f"  English: n = {len(eng_time)}, Mean = {eng_time.mean():.4f}, Std = {eng_time.std():.4f}")
print(f"  Spanish: n = {len(spa_time)}, Mean = {spa_time.mean():.4f}, Std = {spa_time.std():.4f}")
print(f"  French:  n = {len(fre_time)}, Mean = {fre_time.mean():.4f}, Std = {fre_time.std():.4f}")

# --- Assumption Check 1: Normality (Shapiro-Wilk Test) ---
print("\n--- Normality Check (Shapiro-Wilk Test) ---")
for name, data in [('English', eng_time), ('Spanish', spa_time), ('French', fre_time)]:
    if len(data) >= 3:
        stat, p = shapiro(data)
        result = 'Normal' if p > 0.05 else 'Not Normal'
        print(f"  {name:8s}: W = {stat:.4f}, p-value = {p:.4f} → {result}")

# --- Assumption Check 2: Homogeneity of Variances (Levene's Test) ---
print("\n--- Homogeneity of Variances (Levene's Test) ---")
stat_l, p_l = levene(eng_time, spa_time, fre_time)
print(f"  Levene's statistic = {stat_l:.4f}, p-value = {p_l:.4f}")
print(f"  → {'Equal variances assumed' if p_l > 0.05 else 'Unequal variances — consider Kruskal-Wallis test'}")

  French:  n = 17, Mean = 6.1965, Std = 1.9334

--- Normality Check (Shapiro-Wilk Test) ---

  Spanish : W = 0.9073, p-value = 0.0901 → Normal
  French  : W = 0.9403, p-value = 0.3214 → Normal

--- Homogeneity of Variances (Levene's Test) ---
  Levene's statistic = 0.7736, p-value = 0.4671
  → Equal variances assumed
In [27]:
# --- Performing One-Way ANOVA ---
print(f"Selected Test: One-Way ANOVA")
print(f"Significance Level: α = 0.05\n")

f_stat, p_value = f_oneway(eng_time, spa_time, fre_time)

print(f"--- Test Results ---")
print(f"  F-statistic: {f_stat:.4f}")
print(f"  p-value:     {p_value:.6f}")

# Also running Kruskal-Wallis as a non-parametric alternative for robustness
h_stat, p_kw = kruskal(eng_time, spa_time, fre_time)
print(f"\n--- Non-Parametric Alternative: Kruskal-Wallis Test ---")
print(f"  H-statistic: {h_stat:.4f}")
print(f"  p-value:     {p_kw:.6f}")

# --- Inference ---
print(f"\n--- Inference ---")
if p_value < 0.05:
    print(f"  Since the ANOVA p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is LESS than α (0.05),")
    print(f"  we REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✓ Conclusion: At 5% significance level, there is sufficient evidence that")
    print(f"    the mean time spent on the new page DIFFERS across language groups.")
else:
    print(f"  Since the ANOVA p-value ({p_value:.6f}) is GREATER than or equal to α (0.05),")
    print(f"  we FAIL TO REJECT the Null Hypothesis.\n")
    print(f"  ✗ Conclusion: At 5% significance level, there is insufficient evidence to")
    print(f"    conclude that the mean time spent on the new page differs across language")
    print(f"    groups. The time spent appears to be THE SAME across different language users.")

7. Conclusion & Business Recommendations¶

7.1 Summary of Hypothesis Test Results¶

# Question Test Used p-value Decision Conclusion
1 Do users spend more time on the new page? Independent t-test (one-tailed) See above Reject H₀ Users spend significantly more time on the new page
2 Is the new page conversion rate greater? Two-proportion z-test (one-tailed) See above Reject H₀ New page has a significantly higher conversion rate
3 Does conversion depend on language? Chi-square test of independence See above Fail to reject H₀ Conversion is independent of language preference
4 Is time on new page same across languages? One-way ANOVA See above Fail to reject H₀ Time spent is the same across language groups

7.2 Business Recommendations¶

  1. Deploy the New Landing Page Immediately: Both statistical tests (time spent and conversion rate) provide strong evidence that the new landing page outperforms the old one. The new page should be rolled out as the default for all users.

  2. Uniform Design Across Languages: Since conversion does not depend on language preference (Test 3) and time spent is consistent across languages (Test 4), the same landing page design can be confidently deployed across all three language versions without language-specific modifications.

  3. Capitalize on Higher Engagement: The increased time users spend on the new page creates opportunities for:

    • Better ad placement and higher ad revenue
    • More content recommendations to deepen engagement
    • Cross-selling premium subscription tiers

  4. Scale Up the A/B Testing Practice: The success of this experiment validates the A/B testing methodology. E-News Express should adopt continuous A/B testing for:

    • Call-to-action (CTA) button designs and placements
    • Subscription pricing page layouts
    • Content recommendation algorithms
    • Email and notification strategies

  5. Monitor Long-Term Performance: After full deployment, track:

    • Subscriber retention rates (do new-page subscribers stay longer?)
    • Churn rates across subscriber cohorts
    • Revenue per subscriber by language segment
    • Page load times and mobile performance

7.3 Limitations¶

  • Sample Size: With only 100 users (50 per group), the statistical power is limited. A larger sample would provide more robust conclusions.
  • Duration: The experiment captures a snapshot in time; seasonal effects and novelty bias (users may spend more time simply because the page is new) are not addressed.
  • Binary Outcome: Conversion is treated as binary. Richer engagement metrics (pages viewed, return visits, time to conversion) would provide deeper insights.
